claims.text: Nanoparticle structural and chemical stability under the stated service regimes is governed by composition.
Nanoparticle structural and chemical stability under the stated service regimes is governed by crystal structure.
Nanoparticle structural and chemical stability under the stated service regimes is governed by defect density.
Composition and crystal structure will be varied systematically while other factors are held constant.
Defect density and crystal structure mediate stability.
A more ordered structure improves nanoparticle stability relative to a random alloy structure.
Lower defect density improves nanoparticle stability.
More ordered, lower-defect nanoparticles will show a 20% stability increase relative to random-alloy nanoparticles.
The proposed relationship applies at 773–1173 K during catalytic operation.
The proposed relationship applies at 473–1923 K during thermoelectric use.
Agreement within 5% between measured and predicted stability for random, high-defect nanoparticles would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prediction concerns a 20% advantage of ordered, low-defect particles over a random-alloy baseline, but the falsification experiment measures only random, high-defect particles. It treats agreement with an unspecified prediction for that baseline as falsification rather than testing whether the predicted comparative advantage is absent.
